newsitem.title: JAMAICA: Government managers shake up Jamaica's Eagle group.
newsitem.headline: Government managers shake up Jamaica's Eagle group.

text.p: The government- appointed managers of Jamaica's Eagle financial group said Friday they will lay off workers and merge several of the group's units in an effort to return to viability.

Bank of Nova Scotia Canada was appointed on March 14 by the state's Financial Sector Adjustment Co (FINSAC) to take temporary management of Eagle. FINSAC is also providing funding to four other major financial groups in trouble.
The new managers said that, as of May 9, 140 employees, 75 percent of them in Eagle Merchant Bank, Jamaica's largest, will be laid off.
In addition, the flagship merchant bank will be merged with and made a division of a smaller commercial bank unit.

The commercial bank fell J$1 billion (US$21 million) into the red with the central bank from a profit of J$120 million as of end-June 1996, fueld in part by bad debts and runs on the bank as the group's future became uncertain.

There was still no word on the fate of Eagle's other units, which include two hotels managed by Holiday Inn, the island's third-largest life insurance company and a Miami investment bank, First Equity.
The group has total assets of some US$300 million.
FINSAC also will raise J$12.3 billion in medium-term bonds with a 20 percent coupon rate, to be placed largely on the local market.

The money will be used to help companies in difficulty -- Mutual Life, Life of Jamaica, Dyoll Life and Island Life -- and, in return, FINSAC will be issued with 12.5 percent preference shares. The shares will not be sold back to the companies, but disposed of on the market to widen the ownership base.
The government has already provided J$12.5 billion (US$356 million) in financial assistance to banks and other companies in difficulties, according to FINSAC officials.

FINSAC was established by government earlier this year to restructure the ailing financial sector, hit hard by slumps in the equities and real estate markets and by tight monetary policies that have brought inflation down to single digits.
FINSAC is expected to take five years to complete its task.
